body: EyeToy: Play is London Studio's PlayStation 2 party-game collection, first released in Europe on 4 July 2003. Bundled with the EyeToy USB camera, it places a live image of the player on the television and asks for movement instead of an ordinary controller input. Twelve short games turn waving, reaching and changing position into visible responses on screen. The person standing in the room becomes part of the playfield. The arrangement makes the basic instruction unusually direct: an object appears near the player's image, and moving towards it is the means of interacting with it.

The camera detects changes in the picture and compares those movements with the objects displayed by the game. A familiar physical action can therefore become an input without requiring a button sequence to be learned first. Good lighting and a clear view matter because the system has to distinguish the player's movement from the background. The short activities make it easy for another person to take a turn, and high scores can be marked with a photograph. The collection connects play to the room around the television instead of asking the player to look entirely beyond it.

Jamie MacDonald directed the project, with Ron Festejo producing and Pete Marshall leading programming. London Studio designed the collection as the first release built around Sony's new camera accessory. North America received it in November 2003 and Japan in February 2004. Later EyeToy games expanded the idea, but Play established its most immediate appeal: the player could recognise their own body inside the game before understanding any of its rules. That clear introduction helped motion-based interaction reach people for whom a conventional controller could otherwise have been the first obstacle.
